name: Algorithmic Colour Grading
title: Algorithmic Colour Grading
answer: Algorithmic colour grading covers the use of software, including machine learning models, to adjust the colour, contrast, tone and mood of moving or still images. It sits between traditional colour correction, which fixes exposure and white balance, and creative grading, which sets a look. The work spans film and television finishing, advertising, photography, game cinematics and generative illustration pipelines. Practitioners include colourists, editors, photographers and artists who increasingly work alongside automated tools rather than replacing their own judgement.

sections.body: Algorithmic colour grading covers the use of software, including machine learning models, to adjust the colour, contrast, tone and mood of moving or still images. It sits between traditional colour correction, which fixes exposure and white balance, and creative grading, which sets a look. The work spans film and television finishing, advertising, photography, game cinematics and generative illustration pipelines. Practitioners include colourists, editors, photographers and artists who increasingly work alongside automated tools rather than replacing their own judgement.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on colour management systems, calibrated reference displays and grading applications such as DaVinci Resolve, Baselight and Adobe Premiere, with plugins and cloud services adding model driven looks. Machine learning components typically run on GPUs, either locally or in hosted rendering environments, and depend on large sets of graded reference frames for training. Files move through standard formats such as OpenEXR, ACES and LUTs, which carry colour transforms between camera, display and delivery. Storage and bandwidth matter because high dynamic range and high resolution footage is heavy.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A colourist starts from a technical pass that normalises footage, then builds a creative look through primary and secondary corrections, windows, keys and curves. Algorithmic tools assist by matching shots, transferring a reference look, segmenting skin, sky or objects, and suggesting grades that a human then refines. Some systems learn from a colourist's prior decisions and apply similar adjustments to new material. The output is judged on a calibrated display and checked against delivery standards for cinema, broadcast or web. Iteration with the director or client remains central to the process.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and provenance questions arise from the reference material used to train look models and from the footage being graded, since licences for stock, film and photographic sources vary widely. Studios and vendors often keep audit trails of LUTs, project files and model versions so a grade can be reproduced or defended. Where a model was trained on copyrighted frames, the legal position is unsettled, and this site tracks 92 active intellectual property lawsuits across AI generally. Colourists also guard against models that embed a signature look without disclosure, and against bias in skin tone handling across different complexions. Contracts and union agreements increasingly address who owns and can reuse a generated grade.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Expect tighter integration between grading software and generative models, so a look can be described in words and applied across a sequence. Real time, on set grading with model assistance is likely to spread as hardware improves. Standards work on colour, metadata and provenance will shape how grades travel between tools and studios. The open questions are authorship, credit and compensation when a model reproduces a colourist's style, and how much of the craft remains a human decision. Adoption will vary by budget and by how much a production values a named colourist.
